newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stable German prices show inflation under control.
newsitem.headline: Stable German prices show inflation under control.

text.p: Stable consumer price data from two key German states, Hesse and Baden-Wuerttemberg, show inflation is well under control and that monetary policy should remain on hold, analysts said on Thursday.

The state statistics office in Hesse said consumer prices rose 1.3 percent year-on-year and were unchanged month-on-month in October, compared with September's 1.2 percent and one percent drop respectively.

Later, the southern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg said prices were unchanged on the month and rose 1.3 percent on the year, compared with a drop of 0.2 percent on the month and an increase of 1.2 percent year-on-year in September.

"We are very happy with the figures from Hesse and Baden-Wuerttemberg, and both figures were within our expectations. The figures are fully on target," said Manuela Preuschl, an economist with DB Research in Frankfurt.
Elanie Heldmann at BfG Bank in Frankfurt said the inflation figures were positive, if a little higher than she had been expecting, but that they limited scope for the Bundesbank to cut rates.

"The figures suggest a decent price environment. It leaves the Bundesbank in a good position to leave rates where they are. There is no real reason for a cut in short-term interest rates. All in all, a positive development," said Heldmann.

Economists had been worried that the increase in oil prices following recent upsets in the Gulf region would lead to higher heating oil prices, which in turn would lead to a rise in the consumer index overall.
While heating oil rose by 38.8 percent, overall energy prices did not leap by as much as might have been expected in the month, increasing only 1.3 percent.
"Higher mineral oil prices helped push rates up," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.

"But the rise in mineral oil prices is not worrying at the moment. We have seen the bottom...for inflation rates, and they could begin edging higher again very, very slowly in the coming months," he said.

This was not something to get overly worried about, however, said Grebe. "On the mineral oil prices, we expect that the winter will not be so very severe and that higher prices will not have a huge impact on the overall index."

Bond market traders said the numbers were exactly in line with expectations and were unfazed by higher petroleum prices. The figures did not move the market appreciably and the overall trend was sideways
A senior Bund trader in Frankfurt said: "Right now the inflation data is still supporting Bundesbank policy of holding short-term rates steady."
